title: Measuring Social Biases of Crowd Workers using Counterfactual Queries
findings: The paper does not contain any findings related to religion, as it is not a subject of the study. The paper's contribution is a proposed method for measuring social biases (like race and gender) in crowd workers.
references: Robert J Fisher and James E Katz. 2000. Social-desirability bias and the validity of self-reported values. Psychology & marketing 17, 2 (2000), 105–120.

Patrick S Forscher, Calvin K Lai, Jordan R Axt, Charles R Ebersole, Michelle Herman, Patricia G Devine, and Brian A Nosek. 2019. A meta-analysis of procedures to change implicit measures. Journal of personality and social psychology 117, 3 (2019), 522.

Sahaj Garg, Vincent Perot, Nicole Limtiaco, Ankur Taly, Ed H Chi, and Alex Beutel. 2019. Counterfactual fairness in text classification through robustness. In Proceedings of the 2019 AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society. 219–226.
Cathy O’neil. 2016. Weapons of math destruction: How big data increases inequality and threatens democracy. Broadway Books.

Jieyu Zhao, Tianlu Wang, Mark Yatskar, Vicente Ordonez, and Kai-Wei Chang. 2017. Men also like shopping: Reducing gender bias amplification using corpus-level constraints. arXiv preprint arXiv:1707.09457 (2017).
measurement_description: The paper does not measure any aspects of faith or religion. It proposes a method to measure social biases like gender and race in human crowd workers.
